subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography — Coasts: Waves, Landforms and Management
description: Reading passages on wave formation, differential erosion, cliff retreat, sediment transport and coastal management. Questions mix retrieval, inference and explanation so students practise both knowledge and interpretation.

data.sourcePassage: Waves begin when wind blows across the surface of the sea. Friction transfers energy from the air to the water, so the water starts to move in a circular rolling motion. The energy travels forwards even though the water itself does not move forwards across the sea. When a wave enters shallow water near the coast, the base of the wave drags against the sea floor. This friction slows the lower part of the wave, but the top continues moving more quickly. The wave becomes steeper and eventually topples over as a breaker. This is why waves often look highest and most dramatic close to the shore.

questions.question: What transfers energy from the wind to the water?
questions.modelAnswer: Friction transfers energy from the wind to the water.

questions.question: Which statement best describes what moves forwards across the sea?
Why does the top of the wave topple over near the shore?
questions.modelAnswer: The base is slowed by friction with the sea floor while the top keeps moving faster, so the wave steepens and breaks.

questions.question: What does this passage suggest about why waves become more dangerous close to the coast?
questions.modelAnswer: It suggests waves become more dangerous because they grow steeper and break as they enter shallow water, concentrating their energy near the shore.

data.sourcePassage: On some coastlines, bands of hard and soft rock lie at right angles to the sea. This is called a discordant coastline. The softer rock is eroded more quickly, so the coastline is worn back to form a bay. Harder rock resists erosion for longer and remains sticking out as a headland. Wave energy is concentrated on the headland, which means caves, arches, stacks and stumps are more likely to develop there. Inside the bay, wave energy is lower because waves are refracted. This encourages deposition, so beaches often build up in bays. A place such as Swanage Bay in Dorset is a useful example of how differential erosion creates contrasting coastal features.

questions.question: What is the name for a coastline where hard and soft rock alternate at right angles to the sea?
questions.modelAnswer: It is called a discordant coastline.

questions.question: Which feature is most likely to form in softer rock?
Why are caves, arches, stacks and stumps more likely to be found on headlands than in bays?
questions.modelAnswer: They are more likely on headlands because harder rock projects into the sea and receives concentrated wave energy and stronger erosion.

questions.question: How does this passage show the link between erosion and deposition on the same coastline?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows erosion is strongest on headlands, while lower-energy conditions in bays allow deposition and beach formation.

data.sourcePassage: At high tide, destructive waves attack the base of a cliff. Over time they cut into the rock and create a wave-cut notch. Weathering weakens the rock above the notch while wave erosion keeps undercutting it from below. Eventually the overhanging section becomes unstable and collapses. The sea carries away the fallen material, so the waves can attack the cliff again. This repeated cycle causes the cliff to retreat inland. As the cliff moves back, it leaves a smooth rocky surface in front of it. This flat area is called a wave-cut platform and is easiest to see at low tide, when the sea has moved away from the base of the cliff.

questions.question: What feature forms first at the base of the cliff?
Why does the cliff collapse?
options: The overhanging rock becomes unstable after undercutting and weathering
Plants grow on top of the cliff
Sediment piles up at the cliff base
questions.modelAnswer: The overhanging rock becomes unstable after undercutting and weathering

questions.question: Why is the removal of collapsed material important in this process?
questions.modelAnswer: It is important because removing the debris exposes the cliff again, allowing waves to continue eroding it and causing further retreat.

questions.question: Why is a wave-cut platform most visible at low tide?
questions.modelAnswer: It is most visible at low tide because the sea has moved away and exposes the flat rocky surface left by cliff retreat.

data.sourceTitle: Moving Sediment and Managing the Coast
data.targetTitle: Moving Sediment and Managing the Coast
data.sourcePassage: Once waves have eroded material from the coast, that sediment can be transported along the shoreline by longshore drift. The swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle because the waves approach from the direction of the prevailing wind. Gravity then pulls the backwash straight down the beach. This creates a zig-zag movement that shifts material along the coast. Because this movement can remove sand from some places and build it up in others, people often try to manage it. Groynes trap sediment, beach nourishment adds more sand, and managed retreat allows some areas to flood naturally. These choices can cause disagreement because residents, tourists, environmentalists and governments may all value the coastline in different ways.

questions.question: What process moves sediment along the coastline in a zig-zag pattern?
questions.modelAnswer: Longshore drift moves sediment along the coastline in a zig-zag pattern.

questions.question: What pulls the backwash straight down the beach?
Why might a groyne help one section of coast but create problems further along the shoreline?
questions.modelAnswer: A groyne traps sediment in one place, which can protect that beach, but it may reduce the amount of sediment reaching beaches further along the coast.

questions.question: Why can coastal management decisions lead to conflict between different groups?
questions.modelAnswer: They can lead to conflict because different groups have different priorities, such as protecting homes, keeping beaches attractive, preserving habitats or limiting costs.
